41: This page continues the '50-Cent Lesson in Persistence' story from the Introduction. Darby recounts witnessing an incident at his uncle's old-fashioned wheat mill where a small black sharecropper's daughter came to collect fifty cents her mother had requested. The uncle barked at her roughly and refused, telling her to go home. The child said 'Yes sir' but did not move. The uncle, increasingly angry, yelled at her again and threatened her with a switch. She still did not budge. The uncle then picked up a barrel stave and started toward her with an expression indicating trouble. Darby held his breath, certain he was about to witness a horrible beating, knowing his uncle's fierce temper and that sharecropper children were not allowed such defiance in those days. When the uncle reached the child, she stepped forward, looked into his eyes, and screamed: 'MY MOMMA'S GOTTA HAVE THAT FIFTY CENTS!' The uncle stopped, laid down the barrel stave, took out a half-dollar, and gave it to her. The child took the money and backed toward the door, never taking her eyes off the man. The uncle sat down and stared into space for more than ten minutes, pondering the whipping he had just taken.
42: Darby was deeply affected by what he witnessed. It was the first time he had seen a black child deliberately master a white adult. He wondered what strange power the child used. Years later, Darby told Hill the story in the same old mill where it occurred. Hill had devoted nearly a quarter-century to studying that same power. Hill explains that the answer is contained in the principles of this book, with sufficient detail for anyone to understand and apply the same force the child stumbled upon accidentally. He tells readers to keep their mind alert for this power, which may appear as an idea, plan, or purpose, or cause them to revisit past failures for lessons. After Hill explained the power to Darby, Darby retraced his 30 years as a life insurance salesman and acknowledged his success was largely due to the lesson from the child. Darby revealed: 'Every time a prospect tried to bow me out without buying, I saw that child standing there in the old mill, her big eyes glaring in defiance, and I said to myself, I've gotta make this sale.' The better portion of all sales he made were after people had said 'NO.'
43: Darby also recalled his mistake of stopping three feet from gold, calling it 'a blessing in disguise' that taught him to keep on regardless of difficulty—a lesson he needed before succeeding in anything. Hill notes that Darby owed his ability to sell over a million dollars of life insurance annually to these two experiences. Hill reflects that life's successes and failures both have roots in simple experiences; Darby's were commonplace yet held the answer to his destiny. He profited because he analyzed them and found their lesson. Hill asks: what of the person without time or inclination to study failure for knowledge leading to success? This book was written to answer that question through 13 steps or principles. He emphasizes that one sound idea is all one needs to achieve success, and the principles described contain the best practical knowledge for creating useful ideas. Hill then makes an astounding claim: 'WHEN RICHES BEGIN TO COME, THEY COME SO QUICKLY, IN SUCH GREAT ABUNDANCE, THAT ONE WONDERS WHERE THEY HAVE BEEN HIDING DURING ALL THOSE LEAN YEARS.' This contradicts the popular belief that riches come only through hard, long work. When you begin to THINK AND GROW RICH, riches begin with a state of mind—with definiteness of purpose and little or no hard work.
44: Hill explains he spent 25 years in research analyzing thousands of people to understand how wealthy people become that way. He draws a parallel to the Great Depression: it started in 1929, reached record economic destruction, and then began fading after FDR took office. Just as a theater usher raises lights so gradually that darkness is 'transmuted' into light before you realize it, the spell of fear in people's minds gradually faded into faith. Hill promises that mastering these principles will similarly improve one's financial status, transmuting everything one touches into an asset. He identifies a main human weakness: familiarity with the word 'impossible.' People know all the rules that won't work and things that cannot be done. This book is for those seeking rules that made others successful. Hill recounts purchasing a fine dictionary and clipping out the word 'impossible'—suggesting readers do the same. He reiterates: success comes to those who become SUCCESS-CONSCIOUS; failure comes to those who become FAILURE-CONSCIOUS. The book's object is to help readers change from failure consciousness to success consciousness. Another weakness is measuring everything by one's own impressions and beliefs—some readers will believe no one can think and grow rich because their thought habits have been steeped in poverty, want, misery, failure, and defeat.
45: Hill illustrates the tendency to judge by one's own limitations with an anecdote about a prominent Asian student at the University of Chicago who, when asked by President William Rainey Harper what impressed him most about Americans, exclaimed 'Your eyes!'—highlighting how people find odd that which is different from themselves. Hill notes that millions look at successful entrepreneurs like Henry Ford and envy their fortune, luck, or genius, but perhaps one person in 100,000 knows the secret of entrepreneurial success, and those who know are too modest to speak of it because of its simplicity. He then tells the Ford V-8 engine story: Ford decided to build an engine with all eight cylinders cast in one block and instructed his engineers to produce it. The engineers agreed unanimously it was impossible. Ford said 'Produce it anyway.' They replied 'it's impossible!' Ford commanded: 'Go ahead, and stay on the job until you succeed, no matter how much time is required.' Six months passed with nothing. Another six months passed—still nothing. The engineers tried every conceivable plan but the thing seemed 'out of the question—impossible!'
46: After a full year, Ford checked with his engineers and they again reported no way to carry out his orders. Ford said simply: 'Go right ahead. I want it, and I'll have it.' They went ahead, and then 'as if by a stroke of magic, the secret was discovered.' Ford's DETERMINATION had won once more. Hill acknowledges the story may not be minutely accurate but the substance is correct. He tells readers to deduce the secret of Ford's millions from this story, noting they won't have to look far. Ford succeeded because he understood and applied the principles of success—one being DESIRE, knowing what you want. Hill says if readers can identify the principles that made Ford rich, they can equal his achievements in any suited calling. Hill then introduces the concept of being 'Master of Your Fate, Captain of Your Soul,' referencing poet William Ernest Henley's famous lines. He argues Henley should have informed us that we ARE the masters because we have the power to control our thoughts. The universe is a form of energy filled with universal power that adapts to the nature of thoughts we hold and influences us to transmute thoughts into physical equivalent. Critically, this power makes no distinction between destructive and constructive thoughts—it will translate poverty thoughts just as quickly as riches thoughts. Our brains become 'magnetized' with dominating thoughts, attracting forces, people, and circumstances that harmonize with those thoughts.
47: Hill continues explaining that before accumulating riches, we must magnetize our minds with intense DESIRE for riches, becoming 'money conscious' until the desire drives us to create definite plans. Henley, being a poet rather than philosopher, stated the truth poetically but left philosophical interpretation to followers. Hill asserts the principles in this book hold the secret of mastery over economic fate. He prepares readers for the first of the 13 Steps to Riches, urging open-mindedness and noting the principles were gathered from life experiences of 500+ people who accumulated huge fortunes starting from poverty, with little education and no influence. He previews that the next chapter conveys factual information that could change one's entire financial destiny, as it did for two people: his closest personal friend of 25+ years and his own son. He mentions delivering the commencement address at Salem College in Salem, West Virginia, where he emphasized the principle with such intensity that a graduating class member appropriated it and made it part of his philosophy, going on to become a distinguished member of Congress.
48: Hill reveals that the graduating student was Senator Jennings Randolph, who wrote him a letter just before the book went to publisher. The letter is published as a 'foreword' to Chapter 1. Randolph writes that his congressional service gave him insight into people's problems and offers a suggestion that may help thousands. He recalls Hill's Salem College commencement address planting an idea responsible for his opportunity to serve his state and whatever future success he may have. Randolph suggests Hill put into a book the substance of that address, giving Americans the opportunity to profit from his years of experience and association with those who made America the richest nation on earth. He recalls Hill's description of how Henry Ford, with little schooling, no money, and no influential friends, rose to great heights—and how he made up his mind during that speech to make a place for himself regardless of difficulties. Randolph predicts thousands of young people finishing school will seek just such practical encouragement.
49: Randolph's letter continues, urging Hill to include a Personal Analysis Chart with every book so purchasers can do a complete self-inventory indicating what stands in the way of success. He calls such a service 'priceless,' providing readers with an unbiased picture of faults and virtues that would mean the difference between success and failure. Randolph notes millions face the problem of staging a comeback and would welcome Hill's suggestions, speaking from personal experience. He describes thousands of Americans who want to know how to convert ideas into money, starting from scratch without finances. He requests the first copy off the press, personally autographed. The letter is signed 'Cordially yours, JENNINGS RANDOLPH.' Hill notes that what the commencement address kindled in Randolph was his first real understanding of the enormous power of DESIRE—The First Step to Riches.
50: This page features a single inspirational quote in large text: 'A BURNING DESIRE TO BE AND TO DO is the starting point from which the dreamer must take off. Dreams are not born of indifference, laziness, or lack of ambition.' This quote, attributed to Napoleon Hill, serves as a thematic epigraph introducing Chapter 1 on DESIRE. It encapsulates the core principle that achievement requires not passive wishing but an active, consuming desire combined with determination to act. The page functions as a motivational divider between the Introduction and Chapter 1.
